# Comparative institutional practice {#sec-institutional-practice}

Hospital stars, clinical benefit–risk summaries, deprivation ranks and employer report cards all compare units, but the comparisons serve different decisions. Stars combine measurement, aggregation, peer comparisons and a safety condition; benefit–risk analysis relates uncertain outcomes to patient preferences and regulatory decisions. Spatial indicators summarize places before funding programs apply selection filters and constraints, while employer report cards communicate evidence of differential treatment. We examine how these uses determine the meaning of each report.

The cases include operating rules, methodological proposals and empirical studies of reporting specifications, with different objectives, comparisons and supporting evidence. Some studies establish changes in labels without evaluating effects on care, access or treatment. Existing procedures may also address uncertainty and legitimate policy objectives through means other than posterior expected loss; these features must be retained in comparisons with an alternative report.

Hospital stars summarize eligible hospitals; the clinical panel concerns a modeled treatment decision aid; deprivation ranks describe LSOAs before additional MSOA selection rules enter; and employer grades are public research reports with separately proposed institutional uses. The dated case definitions and their evidence are documented in Chapter 3. The common descriptive fields establish no equivalence of preferences, regulatory status or effects on outcomes. ## Hospital stars: aggregation, comparison groups, and a safety constraint {#sec-cms-hospital-stars}

The United States Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Overall Hospital Quality Star Rating illustrates how a compact institutional report can combine several different decisions. Its immediate purpose is to summarize publicly reported information for patients and consumers. The unit receiving the report is an eligible hospital providing acute inpatient or outpatient care; the output is one to five whole stars. This is the **Overall Hospital Quality** system, distinct from CMS ratings for nursing homes, dialysis facilities, insurance plans, and the separate patient-experience star ratings. The case examined here is the April 2026 methodology, version 5.1, prepared for CMS by the Yale New Haven Health Services Corporation's Center for Outcomes Research and Evaluation. The report describes an implemented procedure [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 7–10].

Version 5.1 describes the April 2026 rating using measure data from the October 2025 Care Compare refresh. The dates identify the rating cycle and public input-data release; observation periods vary by measure. The substantive change from the previous methodology is a patient-safety cap, and the report records a transition from SAS to R. Version 5.1 retains version 5.0's methodology while clarifying cluster ranges. A further safety adjustment is anticipated for 2027 and is therefore separate from the 2026 rule [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 7, 11–14].

The initial construction is a composite of available measure scores. Fifty-two measures met the inclusion criteria in this release. CMS standardizes each measure across hospitals and reverses direction when necessary so that higher standardized values represent better measured performance. Measures are assigned to five groups: Mortality, Safety of Care, Readmission, Patient Experience, and Timely and Effective Care. Within a hospital and group, the available standardized scores receive equal weight. The resulting group averages are standardized again before being combined. The base group weights are 22 percent each for the first four groups and 12 percent for Timely and Effective Care [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 14–19].

The report relates the heavier weights for the first four groups to their importance and stakeholder judgments. Standardization permits numerical combination, but equal standard deviations in different domains need not have equal substantive value. Equal weighting within a group also depends on the measures available for each hospital: a measure contributes one third of a three-measure average and one eighth of an eight-measure average. Missing-group weights are redistributed proportionately among available groups. Consequently, the same star label can summarize different evidence and different effective contributions from individual measures [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 17–20].

Eligibility for a star rating depends on a separate reporting threshold. To receive stars, a hospital must have at least three measures in each of at least three groups, including Mortality or Safety of Care. Once that condition is met, all available measures contribute, including groups containing only one or two measures. Thus, the threshold is not a requirement that every contributing group contain three measures. It determines eligibility for the overall report; it does not directly select a high-performing hospital. Hospitals passing the threshold are then assigned to a peer group according to whether three, four, or five measure groups contain at least three measures. This peer assignment does not simply count how many groups have any information [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 21–22].

Within each peer group, CMS applies **k-means clustering** to the continuous summary scores with five clusters, as specified in Step 8 of the 2026 methodology. Hospitals are grouped by proximity to cluster means, and ordered clusters give the initial one-to-five-star classification. The report describes iteration to convergence without establishing a general global-optimality guarantee. Cluster boundaries depend on the peer-group score distribution rather than assigning one fifth of hospitals to every category [@CMSHospitalStars2026, p. 23].

Three types of threshold enter the procedure: minimum information for receiving stars, cluster boundaries that compress the summary score, and a safety condition on the final rating. Raising the information threshold can remove hospitals and alter the comparison set. A change in clustering can recategorize an unchanged score, while a change in the safety condition can alter the final star without changing its initial cluster. The effects of these thresholds therefore need to be considered separately.

The safety condition further restricts the highest label that a hospital can receive. In 2026, a hospital with at least three Safety of Care measures and a score in the lowest safety quartile can receive at most four stars. The quartiles are calculated using all hospitals with at least one Safety of Care measure, including hospitals ineligible for an overall rating. They are therefore not quartiles computed separately within the three rating peer groups. A hospital initially placed in the highest summary-score cluster receives four stars if subject to this cap; hospitals with only one or two safety measures are exempt from it. CMS reports that the cap affected 15 hospitals in this release [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 24, 29–30].

For hospitals meeting the low-safety condition, performance elsewhere cannot produce five stars. The cap thus limits compensation across dimensions when assigning the highest public label. Its minimum-measure condition and relative safety threshold have separate roles, neither of which specifies a posterior probability of unsafe care or a criterionwise expected-error constraint. Since the cap also gives no guarantee for future outcomes, comparing it with a compensatory composite requires consideration of the substantive preference as well as statistical estimation.

Peer-group clustering and the subsequent safety cap mean that the final stars need not follow a single national ordering of the summary score. In Table 8, the observed five-star-cluster score ranges begin at 0.678, 0.703, and 0.425 for the three-, four-, and five-group peers, respectively, before the safety adjustment. These observed ranges are not universal clinical thresholds, and rounded endpoints cannot replace the calculation code. A proposed posterior alternative could replace within-peer classification, the national display, the safety restriction or a combination, depending on the reporting problem [@CMSHospitalStars2026, p. 29].

Gettel and colleagues investigate the role of peer grouping by recalculating ratings for 3,076 hospitals from January 2023 Care Compare data. They retain the scoring method and compare classifications with and without peer groups. Ratings differ for 585 hospitals, or 19.0 percent: peer grouping gives 517 a higher rating and 68 a lower rating, with no difference exceeding one star. This fixed-dataset comparison establishes an effect of the reporting specification on labels. The authors assess agreement without cross-validating which procedure is more accurate or evaluating improved patient care. Their 2023 comparison also predates the 2026 safety cap and measure changes [@GettelEtAl2024, Methods, Results, and Limitations].

The nine-step 2026 assignment procedure uses reported measures, group-score averages, a weighted summary, information thresholds, clustering and the safety condition. At this assignment stage, the report specifies neither a joint posterior for latent hospital qualities nor an expected-loss objective for incorrect cross-star directions. This description is confined to the grading stage; the underlying measures can involve further statistical work. For example, the scoring illustration includes a risk-standardized complication measure, and the report separately presents validity and reliability analyses [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 18, 21–24, 31].

Appendix F reproduces tests for the April 2021 methodology using October 2020 data. They compare group-score means between star categories and repeatedly remove ten percent of hospitals before recalculating ratings. Removing hospitals probes sensitivity to the reporting population, rather than repeated sampling of patient outcomes under latent hospital quality. Mean separation between categories also addresses a different question from the correctness of each hospital-to-hospital direction. We therefore interpret these checks as evidence of category separation and stability under the stated perturbations [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 47–48].

He, Selck, and Normand provide a complementary methodological distinction. Their 2014 article analyzes two-tier classification under a one-way normal random-effects model with unequal hospital sample sizes. It compares classifications based on direct estimates, shrinkage estimates, and posterior probabilities, evaluating sensitivity and specificity against latent performance tiers. It also distinguishes an absolute performance threshold from a relative rule selecting a specified fraction of hospitals. Their framework makes explicit that estimating performance and deciding which institutions to classify as top performers are different tasks. Their model-based accuracy results are not estimates of error in the April 2026 CMS stars, and their relative top-tier selection rule is not CMS's five-cluster procedure [@HeSelckNormand2014, §§2.1–2.2, 6].

The interpretation of whole stars depends on the indicators, weights, eligible population, peer groups and safety cap. Hospitals with the same stars can have different underlying qualities, while those with different stars can be ordered differently on individual components. CMS accordingly advises readers to consider individual measures alongside the overall rating [@CMSHospitalStars2026, p. 24]. Analysing cross-category directions as a decision problem would require a target, comparison population, treatment of the safety preference and assessment of directional uncertainty. Better performance on this statistical objective would leave effects on patient choices, allocation and health outcomes to be evaluated.

## Clinical benefit–risk: outcomes, preferences and their sources {#sec-clinical-benefit-risk}

A treatment can improve one outcome while worsening another, and patients may value the trade-off differently. Comparing treatments therefore requires accounting for both uncertainty about their consequences and preferences over those consequences. For each decision, we must specify the population, outcomes and values assigned to changes in outcomes. The clinical example illustrates these requirements for an action that differs from institutional grading.

FDA's October 2023 final guidance describes its qualitative Benefit-Risk Framework, which organizes therapeutic context, benefits, risks and risk management alongside evidence, uncertainty and reasons for judgment. Integration into CBER clinical-review templates dates to 2013 and into CDER clinical-review and decisional templates to 2015. The guidance prescribes no particular additional analytical method; numerical analyses can inform the regulatory conclusion [@fda2023benefitrisk, pp. 7–8, 19–20]. Thus, the implemented framework provides context for probabilistic multicriteria methods, while actual regulatory or clinical use of a particular algorithm requires separate evidence.

Li and colleagues illustrate benefit–risk analysis by reanalysing creatine trial data in Parkinson's disease. The original NET-PD LS-1 randomized trial enrolled 1,741 participants with early, treated disease at 45 United States and Canadian sites. It compared creatine, 10 grams daily, with placebo alongside dopaminergic therapy. At a planned interim analysis, the monitoring board recommended stopping for futility, and NINDS accepted the recommendation in September 2013. Median follow-up was four years. The investigators concluded that the findings did not support creatine in this population [@netpd2015creatine, pp. 584, 586, 591]. The later methodological illustration uses these data without documenting a new approval, prescribing policy or reversal of the trial conclusion.

Li and colleagues analyzed 1,652 participants with complete covariates and combined five efficacy measures with five selected safety outcomes. The efficacy measures address daily functioning, disease-related quality of life, ambulatory capacity, neurological performance, and disability; the safety criteria include increased blood creatinine, weight gain, oedema, muscle spasms, and diarrhoea. The study therefore presents a concrete problem of comparing unlike outcomes, rather than merely combining several noisy measures of the same attribute. Its multidimensional latent-trait model accommodates continuous and binary outcomes and represents their dependence through shared latent variables. Bayesian estimation supplies distributions for predicted criteria under each treatment, which are then passed to stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis, or SMAA [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3041–3045, 3052]. The authors use their chosen latent structure to predict outcomes; the illustration does not establish that the structure or predictions are correct for every patient.

The preference step changes the target of comparison. In case-specific notation, let $z_{htk}$ denote criterion $k$ for patient $h$ under treatment $t$, and let $v_k$ map that criterion onto a common desirability scale. The paper's additive score can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_{ht}&=\sum_{k=1}^{K} a_{hk}v_k(z_{htk}),\\
a_{hk}&\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{hk}=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here a larger score represents a preferred benefit–risk balance. The coefficients are *swing weights*: they value a change between specified worst and best criterion levels. Their meaning therefore depends on those levels and the value functions, not just on an outcome's name. Li and colleagues use linear value functions and common scaling limits across patients and treatments [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3042–3043]. The score permits compensation: an improvement on one criterion can offset deterioration on another according to the stated preferences. It is consequently a cardinal trade-off model, not a weighted count of which treatment wins more individual criteria. The difference between valuing outcome swings and counting criterion wins matters when weights are used in another decision problem.

For two selected patients, a clinician supplied initial swing weights, with the same elicited vector assumed for both patients. Li and colleagues placed a Dirichlet distribution around that vector to represent imprecision, using concentration one at baseline and examining other concentrations. The patients had different baseline disease scores; creatine's reported first-rank acceptability was 0.68 for one and 0.48 for the other [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3046–3047, Figure 2]. These probabilities summarize modeled clinical predictions and the preference distribution. They are distinct from elicited choice probabilities or measured health improvements, and the paper does not establish implementation of the suggested choices.

Patient preference data were unavailable for the population illustration. The authors simulated individual preference vectors and concentration parameters while using the clinical dataset for the outcome model. They describe the creatine case as a simplified demonstration rather than a trial designed or powered to assess benefit–risk balance [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3046–3048]. The display therefore combines observed clinical evidence with constructed preferences instead of surveying trial participants' values. FDA similarly distinguishes preference information from substantial evidence of effectiveness: the former cannot compensate for absence of the latter. For submitted preference information, it recommends formal, prespecified studies with broadly representative patients [@fda2023benefitrisk, p. 18].

A single displayed probability can integrate several sources of variation. Sampling and model uncertainty concern the clinical evidence; predictive variation concerns a patient's future outcomes; preference imprecision concerns representation of that patient's trade-offs. Differences between patients may represent substantive variation rather than error. Widening the preference distribution changes the assumed values without adding clinical observations. Individual treatment predictions also require modeling assumptions because a patient is observed under only one randomized treatment. Li and colleagues predict outcomes under alternative treatment indicators and sample weights separately, producing a model-based decision aid rather than a directly observed individual benefit [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3044–3045].

The decision also changes across applications. A patient comparison concerns the consequences preferred by that patient, whereas a regulatory assessment concerns a product, indication, intended population and conditions of use. An institutional grade places units in publicly ordered groups and communicates every cross-grade direction. Utility weights and first-rank acceptability consequently leave the cost of withholding institutional comparisons unspecified. Likewise, sharing a reporting grade does not establish therapeutic interchangeability, equal utility or equal safety.

When constructing common grades, we therefore distinguish a compensatory scalar target from criterion-specific comparisons and specify whose preferences are represented. Elicited preferences, proxy judgments and sensitivity assumptions have different evidential roles. Treatment recommendations, regulatory assessments and public grades can use similar probabilistic inputs while serving different objectives. The conditional results in the creatine example should accordingly be read as a methodological illustration in light of the original trial evidence.

## Spatial deprivation: an index, a public classification, and a funding rule {#sec-spatial-deprivation}

Area deprivation measures summarize several forms of unmet need across places from indicators differing in scale, timing and reliability. England's Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025 (IMD25) illustrates how that summary can inform allocation. Its ranks and deciles describe an official composite; the 2026 Pride in Place expansion uses the composite within a separate selection procedure. Index construction, reporting and investment selection consequently place different demands on the evidence.

Published on 30 October 2025, the English Indices of Deprivation describe 33,755 Lower-layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) using the 2021 geography. The overall IMD combines seven domains assembled from 55 indicators. The designation “2025” identifies the release, rather than a common observation date: the technical report explicitly states that the latest available inputs refer to different periods. Each domain represents a particular dimension of deprivation, while the composite expresses a chosen way of bringing those dimensions together. The underlying measurement is therefore already structured by decisions about eligible indicators, relevant populations, and the temporal evidence available. [@mclennan2025imdtechnical, §§1.2, 3.3; @noble2025imdresearch, §3.2.1]

The domain weights reported in the technical report are 22.5 percent each for income and employment; 13.5 percent each for health and disability, and education, skills and training; and 9.3 percent each for crime, barriers to housing and services, and living environment. These are the displayed percentages, whose rounding should not be confused with a complete implementation specification. Before combination, the domain scores are ranked and transformed to a common exponential distribution. The transformation emphasizes the deprived end and limits the extent to which low deprivation in one dimension offsets high deprivation in another. Both the weights and the transformation encode priorities, so the index differs from a simple average of the original measurements. The report relates the weights to substantive reasoning and indicator robustness, and retains them after consultation and methodological review. [@mclennan2025imdtechnical, §§3.6–3.7, table 3.1, appendix E]

Because the weights express substantive importance as well as judgments about indicator robustness, greater precision alone cannot determine them. Agreement on their importance also leaves uncertainty about the measurements. Fitted coefficients could preserve the meaning of deprivation only if the fitting objective were justified in relation to that meaning. We must therefore distinguish the choice and valuation of dimensions from the evidence about places on those dimensions.

The official methodology uses empirical Bayesian shrinkage to stabilize many small-area indicators, combining local information with a larger grouping. In the 2025 revision, the parent grouping generally consists of LSOAs in the same sociodemographic supergroup within a local authority district. Specified education and health indicators retain the local authority grouping because their construction in a secure environment preceded the revised classification. Some indicators and singleton groups are not shrunk. For proportions, appendix C describes empirical-logit-scale shrinkage, with greater movement where local precision is lower relative to between-area variation. This stabilization forms part of the implemented estimation procedure. [@mclennan2025imdtechnical, §3.4, appendix C, especially footnote 100]

The estimated scores are used to rank LSOAs from 1, most deprived, to 33,755, least deprived. Deciles summarize relative position, with decile 1 denoting the most deprived tenth. They allow unequal increments of deprivation and different needs within a band. The research report cautions that area descriptions do not characterize every resident and that low deprivation need not mean affluence. Rank changes between releases also depend on changes in methods, indicators and geography. A decile transition alone therefore identifies neither absolute changes in living conditions nor effects of local interventions. [@noble2025imdresearch, §§3.2.1–3.2.10]

The funding consequence is particularly concrete in the Pride in Place expansion methodology published on 20 March 2026. It identifies 40 additional English neighbourhoods for £20 million each over ten years. For selection, neighbourhoods are represented by 2021 Middle layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs). IMD25 and the Community Needs Index 2023 are separately aggregated from LSOAs using population-weighted averages; their MSOA scores are standardized across England and combined with equal weight. The selection procedure then applies an across-round parliamentary constituency cap and restricts eligibility to MSOAs within the fifth of local authorities with the weakest community cohesion. That filter uses the local percentage agreeing that neighbours pull together in the 2024/25 Community Life Survey. Forty eligible MSOAs are selected in order of the combined need score, and the note names the selected places. This is a documented allocation rule; the note does not establish realized expenditure or effects on residents. [@mhclg2026prideexpansion, “Overview,” “Methodological principles,” and steps 1–5]

Funding allocation introduces further judgments. Population-weighted aggregation changes the geographic unit, combination with community need changes the target, and the cohesion filter restricts eligibility. The constituency cap additionally distributes funding geographically. A highly deprived place may therefore receive no allocation without contradicting its deprivation rank. Treating selected and nonselected places as two deprivation grades would assert a comparison absent from the allocation rule.

Shrinkage reduces the influence of unstable components, while uncertainty in the final composite ordering requires propagation through later calculations. The output inventory lists scores, ranks, deciles, denominators and indicators; the selection note gives calculations and filters. These documents supply no joint propagation into final decile membership or program selection. This account is confined to the described procedure; the inputs and other agency uses may contain uncertainty information. Sensitivity to alternative weights likewise addresses a different question from uncertainty about local component estimates. [@mclennan2025imdtechnical, appendices C and L; @mhclg2026prideexpansion, steps 1–5]

To assess deprivation comparisons under a posterior distribution, we would specify the composite, geography and dependence among component estimates and propagate uncertainty into the reported directions. Investment decisions additionally require a budget, eligibility filters and geographic constraints. Common grades could inform these decisions alongside the existing allocation rule. In either application, domains and weights require substantive justification, and program effectiveness requires evidence beyond the selection ranking. The statistical analysis must therefore be tied to the particular public action.

## Employer discrimination report cards: public comparisons and institutional use {#sec-employer-reporting}

Kline, Rose, and Walters use a correspondence experiment to compare named employers publicly. Their 2024 article reports grades for 97 United States firms alongside contact-disparity estimates and uncertainty. A companion Becker Friedman Institute research brief is dated April 8, 2024, and the final article appeared in the August 2024 *American Economic Review*. The brief identifies its basis as the working paper [@bfi2024discriminationreportcard; @kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2472–2476]. These records establish public disclosure of research findings rather than adoption of the grading rule by a regulator.

The experimental population matters. Beginning with the 2018 Fortune 500 list, the researchers selected 108 firms whose geographically dispersed entry-level vacancies and hiring platforms could be audited. Five application waves ran from October 2019 to April 2021. The overall experiment involved roughly 84,000 applications to 11,000 jobs. Names signaling race were randomly assigned within application pairs, gender-distinctive names were randomized, and other applicant characteristics varied independently. The outcome was attempted employer contact within 30 days, recorded through the fictitious applicants' telephone and email accounts [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2476–2477]. It measures an initial recruitment response under the audit design, rather than completed hiring, pay, promotion, or every dimension of workplace treatment.

The reporting sample excludes eleven firms with contact rates below three percent or fewer than 40 sampled jobs, which the authors considered problematic for contact-ratio estimation. It contains 97 firms, 10,453 jobs, and 78,910 applications [@kline_discrimination_2024, p. 2495, Table 2]. Firms are the reporting units, and vacancies and applications supply their evidence. Selection of auditable firms and these exclusions limit representativeness for American employers as a whole. The 2024 publication also describes an earlier observation period rather than continuously measuring current conduct.

The published displays communicate several things simultaneously. In the baseline racial report card, Figure 7 lists firms, orders them by the authors' granular ranking, and plots empirical Bayes posterior means with 95 percent credible intervals. Colors and symbols identify three star grades. Figure 8 adds industry information and produces four grades under the same reporting preference. Federal contractor status is separately encoded in the labels, using information dated September 2020 [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2504–2508, Figs. 7–8]. The stars therefore accompany estimates and uncertainty; they do not replace all the information with an unexplained category.

A shared grade withholds a directional comparison between two firms while allowing different underlying discrimination levels. Establishing equivalence within a substantive margin would require another statement. Different grades communicate an ordering with uncertainty about its directions. The authors also distinguish relative standing from absolute standards: a favorable racial grade is compatible with bias, and an unfavorable grade alone establishes no specified level of misconduct [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2477, 2506]. Familiar star symbols are therefore interpreted as relative comparisons rather than certification.

The baseline racial display uses an empirical Bayes model that rules out bias against White names. The authors note that this restriction gives positive credible-interval lower limits [@kline_discrimination_2024, p. 2504]. The intervals are consequently conditional on that assumption rather than evidence covering every possible disparity direction. Industry information changes both estimates and categories. Our account describes the model and reporting choices without reproducing the model or independently verifying its numerical error calculations.

Race and gender have separate reports. The gender display separates firms favoring male names from those favoring female names, with a large middle group. Its baseline has four grades and its industry-informed version has five [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2517–2519, Figs. 14–15]. The axis and legend determine the comparison represented by each star count. These separate targets do not form an empirically validated common scale of racial and gender disparities or overall employment fairness.

The authors suggest using the results to direct compliance investigations and anticipate possible responses by employees, customers and organizational leaders. They state that their estimates are not legal assessments of antidiscrimination violations [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2475–2476]. The discussion situates agencies and federal contractors at the time of publication. It proposes routes from information to action without documenting an enforced grade-based investigation policy or measuring corporate responses to these grades.

Between-firm differences may suggest organizational practices to investigate, but the grades alone do not identify which practices caused the results. The authors leave further work to establish recruiting reforms that improve fairness and efficiency [@kline_discrimination_2024, pp. 2522–2523]. Using the evidence to allocate investigations would introduce resources, evidentiary requirements and consequences beyond those of publishing the comparison.

We propose common grades for several criteria with differing evidence and priorities. The report would select coherent directions under a specified rule and uncertainty assessment, withholding comparisons within each grade. The allocation of investigations, legal determinations and choice of recruiting reforms would remain separate decisions. Although the multiple comparisons already encountered by public readers motivate this extension, its effect on their decisions remains to be evaluated; the existing cards do not establish that effect.

## Institutional decisions and the mathematical formulation {#why-institutional-differences-remain-part-of-the-theory}

All these decisions use imperfect multidimensional information, but their units, feasible actions, priorities and probability laws differ. Hospital report eligibility and performance categories answer different questions; a patient's preferences need not equal another population's average utility. Neighborhood ranks leave individual circumstances unresolved, and firm reports leave individual legal claims to adjudication. The mathematical formulation must be interpreted for the unit and decision in each application.

In @sec-measurement-values we examine the meaning of the indicators and intended comparisons, before defining targets, uncertainty distributions and actions in @sec-targets-actions-laws. The cases provide motivation and concrete comparators; the loss and weights still need to be specified. Statistical accuracy under such a specification also differs from improved outcomes following institutional use, which have not been established for the proposed grades.
